newsitem.title: FRANCE: New Paris government sends more troops to Congo.
newsitem.headline: New Paris government sends more troops to Congo.

text.p: France's new leftist government, in its first foreign crisis, said on Sunday it was more than doubling its forces in Congo Brazzaville following the death of one of its soldiers in a firefight and threats to its nationals.

"The government, along with the president (Jacques Chirac) will do all we can to assure the safety of our nationals in Brazzaville," Prime Minister Lionel Jospin told reporters during a visit to the southwestern village of Cintegabelle.

Catherine Trautmann, spokeswoman for the new government which took office just last week, said the decision to send 500 more soldiers to the former French colony had been made jointly by the prime minister's office and the Foreign Ministry.

"The prime minister has been kept informed of developments on a regular basis," Trautmann told Radio Luxembourg. "What would be desirable would be for France to contribute to the stability of this country."

Brazzaville, the Congolese capital, lies just across the river from Laurent Kabila's much larger Democratic Republic of the Congo. The French troops would be flown in from French bases in nearby African states where they are now stationed, Foreign Ministry spokesman Yves Doutriaux said.

There are already about 450 French soldiers in the Brazzaville area, stationed there months ago in case they were needed to evacuate French nationals from nearby Kinshasa during the final days of the civil war that brought Kabila to power in what was then Zaire.
Jospin offered his condolences to the family of the French soldier shot dead in Brazzaville on Saturday evening.

Another five French soldiers were wounded, two of them seriously, in the clash with a band of irregular soldiers as they attempted to evacuate a group of foreigners from a building where they were pinned down.
A senior officer in the Congolese army, who was taking part in the mission, was also wounded in the clash, the French Defence Ministry said.

Brazzaville has been shaken by four days of clashes pitting supporters of former president Denis Sassou Nguesso against soldiers loyal to President Pascal Lissouba and other political and ethnic rivals.
Doutriaux said France wanted a ceasefire in the conflict, followed by a negotiated settlement.

In the meantime, he said about a hundred of the 2,200 French nationals in the Brazzaville area had been taken from their homes to safe areas because of anti-French sentiment and outbreaks of violence and looting in the capital.
Doutriaux advised all other French citizens to remain in their homes and keep in close contact with the embassy.
An Air France plane carrying 78 people fleeing Brazzaville, most of them French citizens, arrived in Paris overnight, and one of those on board said it was "open season on the French" in Brazzaville.

"We did not want to leave, as we did not want to lose everything, but it became necessary. We were threatened with knives and machetes because we were French," one man told France Info radio on landing in Paris.
Some of those on board had come to the airport with nothing but the clothes they wore. One man arrived without shoes, witnesses said.
The commander of French forces in Congo described a chaotic and deadly situation in the streets of Brazzaville.

"The problem is that there are Nguesso's militias and there are Congolese army units which are not under the control of their officers, and so we have seen Congolese troops firing on their fellow soldiers," Commander Alexis Jaraud said.
"There is shooting in the streets, and they are using rocket-launchers in residential neighbourhoods," Jaraud told French television LCI by telephone.
